summary: Gives instructions to IANA and the initial contents of the registries of assigned numbers used by the Secure Shell protocol. It is meant only for setting up the registries referenced by the set of SSH documents. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Every SSH message type and option gets a number. This memo is the official first page of that numbering book.

questions: what are the ssh assigned numbers
what is the ssh private use range
subtitle: The starting contents and rules of the IANA registries for SSH message numbers, reason codes, terminal modes and algorithm names.

tldr.problem: The SSH protocol documents use many numbers and names (messages, error codes, algorithms) that need one shared registry and clear rules for adding more.
tldr.mechanism: This document gives IANA the initial contents of each SSH registry, the naming conventions, and the allocation policy for future entries, such as Standards Action or IETF Consensus, with ranges kept for private use.
tldr.outcome: It defines no new protocol. It is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8268, RFC 9142 and RFC 9519.

today: RFC 4250 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8268, RFC 9142 and RFC 9519, so the live IANA registries may differ from the initial tables here. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Purpose and Conventions
sections.content:
This document does not define a new protocol. It creates the initial state of the IANA databases for the SSH protocol and holds the instructions for future assignments. Apart from one HISTORIC algorithm generally regarded as obsolete, it adds nothing that is not already defined in the SSH architecture (RFC 4251), transport (RFC 4253), authentication (RFC 4252) and connection (RFC 4254) documents. Its whole text is the IANA Considerations for SSH.

SSH documents use the RFC 2119 requirement keywords. Namespace allocation words such as PRIVATE USE, FIRST COME FIRST SERVED, EXPERT REVIEW, SPECIFICATION REQUIRED, IESG APPROVAL, IETF CONSENSUS and STANDARDS ACTION follow RFC 2434. The document also fixes a convention: protocol field names appear in single quotes, and example values in double quotes.
sections.eli5: This is not a new game. It is the scoreboard that lists the numbers and names the game already uses, and the rules for adding more.

sections.title: Message Numbers
sections.content:
Every SSH packet starts with a one-byte message number that says what the payload is. Numbers run from 1 to 255 and are split into blocks by protocol layer: 1 to 19 for generic transport messages, 20 to 29 for algorithm negotiation, 30 to 49 for key-exchange-specific messages, 50 to 59 for generic user authentication, 60 to 79 for method-specific authentication, 80 to 89 for generic connection messages and 90 to 127 for channel messages. The range 128 to 191 is reserved for client protocols and 192 to 255 is for local extensions.

The initial table assigns, for example, SSH_MSG_DISCONNECT = 1, SSH_MSG_KEXINIT = 20, SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST = 50, SSH_MSG_GLOBAL_REQUEST = 80, SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN = 90 and SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_DATA = 94.

New numbers in 1 to 29, 50 to 59 and 80 to 127 MUST go through STANDARDS ACTION. Numbers 30 to 49 and 60 to 79 are defined by the key exchange or authentication method. Numbers 128 to 191 need IETF CONSENSUS, and IANA does not control 192 to 255, which is PRIVATE USE.
sections.eli5: Each kind of message wears a number tag. The numbers are grouped like apartment floors, so a number tells you which part of SSH the message belongs to.

sections.title: Reason Codes and Data Types
sections.content:
Three small registries hold 32-bit values. Disconnection reason codes, sent in SSH_MSG_DISCONNECT, run from 1 (SSH_DISCONNECT_HOST_NOT_ALLOWED_TO_CONNECT) to 15 (SSH_DISCONNECT_ILLEGAL_USER_NAME). Channel connection failure codes, sent in SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN_FAILURE, are 1 to 4, from SSH_OPEN_ADMINISTRATIVELY_PROHIBITED to SSH_OPEN_RESOURCE_SHORTAGE. The extended channel data registry has one entry, SSH_EXTENDED_DATA_STDERR = 1.

For all three, new values MUST be assigned sequentially through IETF CONSENSUS, and IANA will not assign anything from 0xFE000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF, which is left for PRIVATE USE.

For channel failure codes the private range is split in two. 0xFE000000 to 0xFEFFFFFF is for locally assigned channel types, such as one named example_session@example.com. If the server does not understand the channel type, it MUST answer with reason code 3. The range starting with 0xFF has no restrictions and is essentially for experimentation.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, SSH says why with a code number, like a teacher's list: 1 means not allowed, 2 means broke the rules. A few numbers at the end are saved for people to invent their own.

sections.title: Pseudo-Terminal Modes
sections.content:
A pty-req channel request MUST include an encoded terminal modes value, which is a byte stream of opcode and argument pairs. Opcodes are one byte long. Opcodes 1 to 159 have a uint32 argument, and 160 to 255 are not yet defined.

The initial table maps opcodes to terminal settings that will look familiar from Unix terminals. Opcode 0 (TTY_OP_END) ends the list, 1 is VINTR (the interrupt character), 53 is ECHO (enable echoing), 91 is CS8 (8 bit mode), 128 is TTY_OP_ISPEED and 129 is TTY_OP_OSPEED (input and output baud rate in bits per second). Not all of these characters are supported on all systems. New opcodes MUST be assigned through IETF CONSENSUS.
sections.eli5: When you ask for a terminal, you can also send a list of settings, like turning the echo of your typing on. Each setting has its own number.

sections.title: Names and Name Spaces
sections.content:
Many SSH registries use text names instead of numbers. Registered names MUST be printable US-ASCII, MUST NOT contain an at-sign, a comma, whitespace, control characters or DEL, are case-sensitive, and MUST NOT be longer than 64 characters. New names MUST go through IETF CONSENSUS.

Names containing an at-sign are locally extensible and are neither registered nor controlled by IANA. They have the form name@domainname, where the part after the at-sign MUST be a fully qualified domain name controlled by whoever defines the name. The RFC gives ourcipher-cbc@example.com as an example, and notes that the resemblance to email addresses is purely coincidental.

The remaining tables list the initial names. Service names: ssh-userauth and ssh-connection. Authentication methods: publickey, password, hostbased and none. Channel types: session, x11, forwarded-tcpip and direct-tcpip. Global requests: tcpip-forward and cancel-tcpip-forward. There are also channel request names such as pty-req, shell, exec and exit-status, a list of signal names such as INT and TERM, and no initial subsystem names.
sections.eli5: Official names have to be short and plain, and a name with an @ and your own website address in it is yours to make up without asking anyone.

sections.title: Key Exchange and Algorithm Names
sections.content:
Key exchange methods start with diffie-hellman-group1-sha1, which uses an Oakley group from RFC 2409, and diffie-hellman-group14-sha1. The RFC says SSH keeps its own group identifier space, so implementations should treat these names as opaque identifiers and not assume a link to the IKE groups.

Encryption algorithm names include 3des-cbc, aes128-cbc, aes192-cbc, aes256-cbc, blowfish-cbc, the Twofish and Serpent families, arcfour, idea-cbc, cast128-cbc and none. The one HISTORIC entry is des-cbc. MAC names are hmac-sha1, hmac-sha1-96, hmac-md5, hmac-md5-96 and none. Public key algorithms are ssh-dss, ssh-rsa, pgp-sign-rsa and pgp-sign-dss. Compression names are none and zlib.

The details of each algorithm are in the transport layer document, RFC 4253. This RFC only fixes the names.
sections.eli5: Each locking method SSH can use gets a nickname, so both sides can say which one they want to use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The section is two sentences. It says the protocol provides a secure encrypted channel over an insecure network, and that full security considerations are in the SSH architecture document, RFC 4251. This registry document adds none of its own.
sections.eli5: This list only lists numbers. The safety rules for SSH are in the main SSH book.

items.label: Transport generic
items.desc: Disconnect, ignore, debug and similar messages.

items.label: Key exchange specific
items.desc: Meaning set by the key exchange method.

items.label: User authentication generic
items.desc: Request, failure, success and banner messages.

items.label: User authentication method specific
items.desc: Meaning set by the authentication method.

items.label: Channel related
items.desc: Open, data, close and requests on a channel.

items.label: Local extensions
items.desc: PRIVATE USE; IANA does not control it.
